story.title: Google will let schools skip AI tools, but they have to give up search, too

facts.text: Google announced on Tuesday that it plans to disable AI tools for K-12 students next year unless school administrators explicitly turn them on.
The tech giant says the change follows consultations with schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers.
As a result, Google is revising its approach across Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search.

Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” which means that if a school chooses to restrict AI altogether, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”
However, Google Search and its AI features are now inseparable.
Given the dominance of Google’s suite of apps in classrooms and the widespread use of Chromebooks, the decision underscores the company’s influence over the education sector.
Google announced the upcoming change alongside the launch of Guided Learning in schools.
The tool, which was unveiled earlier this year, sort of functions like an AI tutor, as it’s designed to help users build a deep understanding instead of just getting answers.
The launch comes amid concerns that AI chatbots undermine the learning process because they spit out direct answers.

Aisha is a consumer news reporter at TechCrunch.
The New York Times earlier reported that schools that turned off AI access entirely would not have access to Google search.

Amid outcry from educators about tech in classrooms, Google said Tuesday that artificial-intelligence tools, including the chatbot Gemini, will be disabled by default on K-12 student accounts, unless administrators choose to turn them on.

A Washington Post-Schar School poll of Kansas voters last week found registered Democrats were more than twice as likely as registered Republicans to complete the survey after answering an interviewer’s call — 32 percent versus 12 percent.
Google search typically includes an AI overview that, if expanded, has a chat window for further questions.
“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) said on X.
“No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.”
Google says the move responds to feedback from parents and teachers who say that AI products have been disastrous for the ability of children to learn and to think critically.
Google did not immediately return a request for comment.
Google is betting that schools won’t want to give up Google Search and will therefore accept AI tools.
This will expose students to AI early and often, possibly changing the way they interact with technology.
Schools that don’t like Google’s approach could switch to alternatives like DuckDuckGo, which lets you disable AI features.
But will Google’s new Guided Learning be enough to assuage their concerns?
Google will offer schools AI tools that purportedly don’t give away the answers.
While Google is trying to move beyond Chromebooks , the ubiquity of these devices has made the company’s education products huge in schools.
Now, Google says it will let educators choose whether to allow its AI tools in the classroom.
However, blocking AI tools also means giving up search, leaving schools with a difficult decision.
Google could make a version of search for schools that doesn’t have AI tools, but it’s not doing that.
Instead, it’s creating two different versions of AI in search.
The latter, available in Classroom as well as search, is supposed to provide one-on-one tutoring and assistance without giving away all the answers.
Google notes all of its generative AI products can make “mistakes,” though, so it may not be difficult to talk the chatbot into doing your homework.
In a statement to The New York Times , Google education VP Chris Phillips reiterated this approach to web search.
Google executives have said in no uncertain terms that Google Search is AI search .
Most searches now provide an AI Overview at the top, and the company is constantly coming up with new ways to nudge people toward the conversational AI Mode chatbot function.
When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear.
The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search .
There’s no picking and choosing—you either allow all the AI or none of it.

Students using Google software in the classroom will not be allowed to access the company’s search engine unless their school system also opts in to artificial intelligence tools, the tech giant said Tuesday.
On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators.
Instead, K-12 schools will be able to individually turn each Google tool on or off – including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search – with each being off by default until administrators turn it on.
But because search is integrated with AI, schools that opt out of AI altogether would also lose access to Google search.
“Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available,” Golin said in a statement.
“Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI.
This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media.
“As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”
\nThis is a space where subscribers can engage with each other and newsroom staff at The Globe and Mail.

Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and “use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.”
All comments are subject to the Community Guidelines and are moderated. \n

The company also said it is updating its search tools to make them “better for learning,” including offering step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to school work.
Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools.
Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform, and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.
But turning off AI altogether is not possible if schools want to use Google products.

New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation’s biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use.
Google has not yet responded to messages seeking additional comments.
